# Write-Only Code

**Sources:**
- [Write-Only Code](https://www.heavybit.com/library/article/write-only-code) - Joseph Ruscio, General Partner at Heavybit, February 2026
- [Agentic Code Review](https://addyosmani.com/blog/agentic-code-review) - Addy Osmani

- [Context engineering, loop engineering, software factories with Dex Horthy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Usufn8IQJgw) - The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, Dex Horthy (founder, HumanLayer)

## Summary

"Write-Only Code" describes an emerging paradigm where substantial amounts of production code are generated by AI agents and never read by humans. Rather than treating this as a failure mode, Ruscio frames it as an inevitable evolution: "humans had to read this" becomes an anti-pattern as organizations develop new mechanisms for trust and accountability that don't depend on manual code review.

## Historical Context: Breaking Bottlenecks

Ruscio draws parallels to previous infrastructure revolutions. When cloud computing eliminated hardware provisioning constraints, developer velocity became the new bottleneck. Now, AI elimination of coding work itself represents the next threshold shift. Each revolution removes the current constraint and reveals the next one.

## From Review to Trust

Instead of relying on human code inspection, organizations will develop new confidence mechanisms:

- **Code reading coverage** - Metrics tracking what percentage of production code humans have actually examined, acknowledging that 100% is no longer realistic or necessary
- **Slop radius management** - Understanding how far unintended behaviors can propagate through a system before being caught
- **Automation-based confidence** - Replacing manual review with automated verification systems (tests, formal methods, runtime monitoring) as the primary trust mechanism

## Engineer Role Transformation

Rather than authors and reviewers, engineers become:

- **Systems designers** - Shaping high-level intent and constraints that guide AI code generation
- **Trade-off managers** - Balancing competing priorities across systems rather than within individual functions
- **Risk reducers** - Building systems that remain correct without requiring comprehensive human understanding of every line

## Core Insight

> "The role of a software engineer has always been to sit between poorly specified, natural-language business goals and mostly deterministic machine behavior."

Responsibility doesn't disappear when code becomes write-only. It evolves toward designing self-correcting systems rather than reviewing every line. The engineer's value shifts from "can write and read code" to "can design systems where correctness is verifiable without reading every line."

## Implications

The challenge isn't whether write-only code arrives, but whether organizations will invest early in new primitives for trust, accountability, and control, or adapt haphazardly under pressure.

## Evidence From the Field: The 3-6 Month Horizon

Dex Horthy ran the experiment. His team built a "lights off" software factory in July 2025 — agents shipping code, nobody reading it — and shut it down by November. His estimate from that experience: it takes about three to six months of shipping with nobody reading the code before you realize the codebase has degraded to the point where starting over is cheaper than fixing it.

The failure mode was concrete. Debugging an issue required three weeks of onboarding back into a codebase the team had stopped reading three months earlier, because no amount of expert prompting could get the model to find the root cause — it turned out to be a primary key threaded through the system that needed to be a different type. Horthy's initial reaction was that the trade was still worth it: occasional two-week manual fixes in exchange for months of not reading code. He no longer believes that, because the volume of generated code has gone up 10x to 100x and the problem scales with it.

His diagnosis is that the models aren't being trained on the thing that matters here. Benchmarks are SWE-bench-shaped — here's a commit, here's an issue, reproduce the fix — and the cost function of bad architecture and bad program design can't be evaluated by running the unit tests, because it hits you three to six months later when the software has become impossible to change. He is also skeptical of agentic code review as the replacement gate: models are sycophantic about code they wrote, and a closed loop of model-writes/model-reviews has correlated blind spots. His preferred move is to spend the human hour earlier — in planning and design, where taste and architectural judgment actually apply — rather than at the PR, and to point loops at improving codebase quality (nightly cron jobs that fix one anti-pattern and open one small PR) rather than at shipping features unread.

This connects to several related concepts in AI engineering:

- **Backpressure for agents** - Write-only code demands stronger automated feedback loops (tests, type systems, linters) since human review is no longer the safety net
- **Context rot** - As codebases grow with AI-generated code, the volume of context that would need to be reviewed exceeds what models (or humans) can reliably process
- **The Bitter Lesson** - General methods (automated verification, runtime monitoring) will outperform human-knowledge approaches (manual code review) as scale increases

## The Review System That Prevents It

Addy Osmani's "Agentic Code Review" is the direct continuation of this argument: where Ruscio names the failure mode, Osmani specifies the system that keeps code from becoming write-only by default. His framing is that generation got cheap while understanding stayed exactly as expensive, so the bottleneck moved from writing to verifying — and verification is now the leveraged skill.

The practical shape he proposes: tier review by risk rather than by author, fast-fail expensive PRs on predictive signals before a human looks, require evidence up front (intent statement, test output, proof of execution), keep diffs small and instruct agents to produce reviewable ones, scrutinize test changes since agents sometimes "fix" tests to match broken behavior, hold CI gates strictly, and keep the merge decision with a human. He describes this as human *on* the loop rather than *in* it — sampling and spot-checking instead of reading every diff — while warning that fully closed model-reviews-model loops are "borrowed confidence" with correlated blind spots.

One mechanism matters especially here: agents reason through decisions and then discard that reasoning, so the reviewer is the first human to see the code with no access to intent. Capturing agent decision logs makes reconstructing that intent cheap enough to be worth doing, which is precisely the "code reading coverage" problem approached from the other end.

## Key Takeaway

Human accountability endures; the mechanisms ensuring it fundamentally change. Organizations that build robust automated verification systems early will thrive in a write-only code world, while those clinging to human review as the sole gatekeeper will be overwhelmed by the volume of AI-generated code.
